node.label: Gareth Stedman Jones
node.date_label: Outcast London 1971 · “Working-Class Culture and Working-Class Politics in London” 1974 · “Class Struggle and the Industrial Revolution” 1975 · “The Language of Chartism” 1982 · Languages of Class 1983 · Foster, Gray, Epstein, Kirk, Scott 1985–87 · Mayfield and Thorne, Lawrence and Taylor 1992–93 · “The Determinist Fix” 1996 · An End to Poverty? 2004 · The Cambridge History of Nineteenth-Century Political Thought 2011 · Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion 2016
node.description: A British historian of nineteenth-century England whose Languages of Class (1983) asked whether 'the working class' had any reality apart from the language in which it was described. Outcast London (1971) and the essays of 1974–75 worked inside Marxist social history: class consciousness tied to control of the labour process, reformism after 1848 explained structurally. The 1983 introduction and 'Rethinking Chartism' (first printed in The Chartist Experience, 1982) dropped the assumption that 'experience' links social being to consciousness: radicalism was 'a vocabulary of political exclusion', Chartism a political movement against a tyrannical state, and the task was to study grievance and aspiration 'within political languages themselves' (pp. 22, 104, as quoted by Foster and Epstein). Foster, Gray, Epstein, Kirk and Joan Scott answered in 1985–87; Mayfield and Thorne, Lawrence and Taylor in 1992–93. He turned to the history of political thought: An End to Poverty? (2004), the Cambridge History of Nineteenth-Century Political Thought (2011) and Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion (2016).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gareth Stedman Jones (b. 1942); Outcast London: A Study in the Relationship between Classes in Victorian Society (1971; Verso 2013); 'Working-Class Culture and Working-Class Politics in London, 1870–1900' (Journal of Social History 7:4, 1974); 'Class Struggle and the Industrial Revolution' (New Left Review I/90, 1975); 'Engels and the Genesis of Marxism' (NLR I/106, 1977); 'The Language of Chartism', in Epstein and Thompson, eds, The Chartist Experience (1982); Languages of Class: Studies in English Working Class History 1832–1982 (1983); 'The Determinist Fix' (History Workshop Journal 42, 1996); 'Anglo-Marxism, Neo-Marxism and the Discursive Approach to History' (1997); An End to Poverty? A Historical Debate (2004); with Ira Katznelson, eds, Religion and the Political Imagination (2010); with Gregory Claeys, eds, The Cambridge History of Nineteenth-Century Political Thought (2011); Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion (2016). Readers: John Foster (1985), Robert Gray (1986), James Epstein (1986), James Cronin (1986), Neville Kirk (1987), Joan W. Scott (1987), David Mayfield and Susan Thorne (1992), Jon Lawrence and Miles Taylor (1993), Geoff Eley and Keith Nield (2000), Zachary Samalin (2017), William Clare Roberts (2019), Peter Gurney (2025).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-22 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-stedman-jones.md and -part2.md): Foster 1985 (NLR, in full, open); Epstein 1986 (Labour/Le Travail, in full, open); Kirk 1987 (pp. 2–5 and 44–47 from the Cambridge Core PDF, with the atlas's earlier pp. 6–7, 14–17, 46–47 and opening notes); the ILWCH 31 editors' remarks on Scott's essay (in full); his 1975 NLR review of Foster (in full, open); the Cambridge Core summaries of the 1983 introduction and of the 2011 Cambridge History introduction; the Mayfield–Thorne abstract; publisher pages for Outcast London and An End to Poverty?; reviews of Karl Marx by Samalin (2017) and Roberts (2019); Gurney 2025 (pp. 2–3); Eley and Nield 2000 (in full, from the spread research). Unread: the Introduction and 'Rethinking Chartism' themselves (pages cited as quoted by Foster, Epstein and Kirk; the atlas's earlier reading of pp. 90–98 and 173–178 came by an unidentified route and is not reused for new wording), Gray 1986, Cronin 1986, Scott's own 1987 text beyond p. 1, Palmer 1990, Dorothy Thompson 1984, Lawrence and Taylor 1993, 'The Determinist Fix' (1996), the 1997 Lüdtke chapter, the 1974 JSH text, the 2004–16 books. Posts rest on institution pages as cited by Wikipedia (not seen) and on the Columbia author note; the Berkeley Townsend Center fellow page (read) gives the NLR board years only as late 1960s–early 1970s, and membership of the HWJ founding collective is unconfirmed, so neither is dated. The 1974 King's fellowship is withheld pending an institutional witness. Born 17 December 1942 (Wikidata); elected FBA 2013 (Wikidata P166; the QMUL news page returned 404).

proposed_edges.relationship: Outcast London (1971), the 1974 essay on London working-class culture and the 1975 review of Foster: class consciousness tied to control of the labour process, the late-Victorian 'remaking' as defensive and conservative, reformism after 1848 explained structurally
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NLR 1975 read in full (sections 'Industrial Struggle', 'Conceptual Problems', 'Balance Sheet'): from Capital he distinguishes struggles over the appropriation of the product from struggles over control of the labour process, the second converging with political demands; Lenin's trade-union/class-consciousness pairing fits Oldham badly; the ebb of struggle after 1848 should be explained by a new structure covering the whole workforce, proposed as 'experimental'. The 1974 essay through Epstein 1986, pp. 204–205 (read): 'justly influential'; 'impermeability … no longer threatening or subversive, but conservative and defensive' (LoC p. 215, as quoted); 'Capitalism had become an immovable horizon' (p. 237, as quoted). Outcast London: Verso description only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Writes inside History Workshop's call for a new history of Labour and socialism — 'Why Is the Labour Party in a Mess?' (1982–83), the 1984 and 1996 HWJ essays — while his language argument remains 'a contested reorientation', not a Workshop doctrine
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Epstein 1986, p. 207 and n. 22 (read): the Labour essay belongs to 'a more general appeal associated with History Workshop for a new kind of history of the Labour Party and socialism', citing the HWJ 12 editorial and Samuel and Stedman Jones (eds), Culture, Ideology and Politics (1982). HWJ 18 (1984) and 42 (1996): bibliographic only. Membership of the founding collective is unconfirmed (HWJ 1:1 editorial signed 'Editorial Collective'; the members not shown). The roster row's role is changed from 'critic' to 'contributor' in revision 1.152; edge_200 (now gareth_stedman_jones → language) carries the argument itself.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chartism read as a political movement: radicalism 'a vocabulary of political exclusion whatever the social character of those excluded', its rise and ebb following the changing 'visage of the state' rather than class formation (1982–83, as quoted by Epstein)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Languages of Class pp. 104, 107, 153, 161, 173–174 as quoted by Epstein 1986, pp. 197–199 (read): radicalism 'a vocabulary of political exclusion whatever the social character of those excluded' and 'it could never be the ideology of a specific class' (p. 104); 'there was no independent rationale within radical ideology for antagonism towards the middle class as such' (p. 107); Chartism 'represented the rapid upsurge and gradual ebbing away of this specific vision of the state' (pp. 173–174). Foster 1985 ('The Language of Chartism', read): 'Chartism was what it was: a movement for parliamentary reform'. Kirk 1987, pp. 3–4 (read): the essays replace the dominant 'social' reading with a political one. Epstein's judgement that the account of the state is 'a major advance' (p. 203) read. The chapter itself: the atlas's existing record (pp. 90–98, 173–178) and the Cambridge Core metadata.

proposed_edges.relationship: From inside the tradition: Lenin's trade-union/class-consciousness pairing fits Oldham badly (1975); by 1983 the 'social being / social consciousness' relation itself is reopened; later, Engels's part in making 'Marxism' (1977, 2016)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NLR 1975 read in full ('Conceptual Problems'): Foster's criterion for revolutionary consciousness is drawn from the period it is meant to prove; Lenin's pairing fits Oldham badly; the early Marx's alienation couplet is called idealist. Languages of Class p. 7 and pp. 19–22 as quoted by Epstein 1986, pp. 195–196 (read), with Epstein's verdict (p. 208): 'One of the great strengths of these essays is the sustained critique of the teleological aspects of Marxist theory'. NLR 1977: page opened (institutional access), thesis from the opening only. Karl Marx (2016) unread; Samalin (2017, read) and Roberts (2019, read) report its argument that the determinist Marx was Engels's and Kautsky's construction, Roberts objecting that it casts Marx as hostile to representation, 'a fundamental distortion'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Moves to the history of political thought: An End to Poverty? (2004) on Paine and Condorcet, the Cambridge History of Nineteenth-Century Political Thought (2011, with Claeys) tracing forms of political language, Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion (2016); Kirk had already called the Chartism essays 'conventional intellectual history' (1987)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Columbia University Press description and author note for An End to Poverty? (read); Cambridge Core introduction summary of the 2011 Cambridge History (read): a systematic account of political and social thought after the French Revolution, tracing 'particular preoccupations' and forms of political language rather than a canon. Samalin (2017, read): the biography strips away the 'retouching' that made Marx a prophet of economic determinism and extends the Chartism thesis of Languages of Class. Kirk 1987, p. 4 n. 6 (read): Stedman Jones offers a history of radicalism as a body of ideas 'in the manner of conventional intellectual history'. The books themselves are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson 'freed' class consciousness from reduction to productive forces but still assumes a 'relatively direct relationship' between social being and consciousness, treating language as the expression of 'experience' (1983, pp. 16–20, 101, as quoted by Foster and Kirk)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Languages of Class p. 101 as quoted by Foster 1985 ('Political Consequences', read in full): Thompson's approach 'still assumes a "relatively direct relationship between 'social being' and 'social consciousness' which leaves little independent space to the ideological context within which the coherence of a particular language of class can be reconstituted"'. Kirk 1987, p. 3 n. 5 and p. 5 n. 8 (read): the criticisms of Edward Thompson in LoC pp. 16–20 are 'brief but unmistakable'; Stedman Jones treats Thompson's 'experience' as subjectivist and implies the Thompsons, Epstein and Sykes treat language too unproblematically as its expression; Dorothy Thompson's work is not addressed directly. Eley and Nield (2000, n. 47, read) make Languages of Class the second of 'three moments' after cultural Marxism. The pages themselves are unread (as quoted by).

proposed_edges.relationship: Stedman Jones presents his own work as taking forward Thompson's redefinition of class — Thompson's 'great achievement' — and Kirk records his 'acknowledged debt' to Thompson's anti-reductionism (1983, as read by Foster and Kirk)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Foster 1985 ('Political Consequences', read in full): 'Stedman Jones sees himself as taking forward the redefinition of class initiated by Thompson, whose "great achievement" is to have "freed the concept of class consciousness from any simple reduction to the development of productive forces … and to have linked it to the development of a political movement which cannot be reduced to the terminology of incoherent protest"' (LoC p. 101, as quoted by Foster). Kirk 1987, p. 3 n. 5 (read): 'despite an acknowledged debt to Thompson's anti-reductionism'. Foster's remark that 'the debate on Chartism's class content was initiated by the publication of Thompson's Making' dates the line. The critique that accompanies the debt is drawn as gareth_stedman_jones → ep_thompson.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott faults 'Rethinking Chartism' for using theories of language 'in an essentially conservative manner': treating language as a vehicle for ideas rather than a system of meaning, and so missing the gendered construction of class (1987, as quoted in the ILWCH editors' remarks)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: ILWCH 31 'Editor's Remarks', pp. v–vi, read in full (open PDF): Scott 'criticizes Gareth Stedman Jones for using theories of language in his "Rethinking Chartism" in an essentially conservative manner'; he 'stops short of opening up … important conceptual questions' because he treats language as a vehicle for communicating ideas rather than as a system of meaning (p. v, the editors quoting her); her rereading of Chartism finds that its linguistic construction of class meant the working class would be represented by men (pp. v–vi). Scott's own pages are unread beyond p. 1 (existing record); her n. 3 cites Languages of Class. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 7, read): 'Prying open Stedman Jones's exegesis, and breaking its silences over gender', and n. 20: his 'only direct rejoinder to Scott', in the 1997 Lüdtke volume (unread), 'grudgingly admits' her point. Evidence standing: editors' summary and a later reader; Scott's text unread.
